lessons.title: Hello, Mainframe
intro: In 1959, a committee led by the US Department of Defense, with Grace Hopper's ideas at its heart, made a language for business: COBOL, the COmmon Business-Oriented Language. It was meant to read like English, so managers could check the programs.

For decades, COBOL ran on IBM mainframes. You typed at a 3270 terminal, sent your program off as a job, and its output came back. Banks, insurers and governments still run billions of lines of it today.

A COBOL program has up to four divisions, always in the same order. The smallest one needs only two: IDENTIFICATION (its name) and PROCEDURE (what it does). DISPLAY shows text, and STOP RUN ends the job.

exercises.explanation: It was made for business: payrolls, bills and bank accounts.
DISPLAY shows the text between the quotes, without the quotes.
COBOL's verb for showing something is DISPLAY.

options: Pauses until a key is pressed

exercises.prompt: Put the lines of the smallest COBOL program in order.
exercises.explanation: First the name, then the procedure with its statements.

exercises.prompt: Who is most connected with COBOL's ideas?
exercises.explanation: Her FLOW-MATIC language, with English words instead of symbols, was COBOL's model.

lessons.title: Columns and Areas
intro: COBOL comes from the punched card, so every column has a job. Columns 1 to 6 hold a sequence number, so a dropped deck could be put back in order. Column 7 holds a * to make the line a comment.
Area A is columns 8 to 11: division headers, paragraph names and 01 levels start there. Area B is column 12 and on: that's where the statements go. Everything after column 72 is ignored.
So a division starts with 7 spaces, a statement with 11. Here, the example also has the sequence numbers the programmers punched in columns 1 to 6.

code: 000300* THIS LINE IS A COMMENT: THE * IS IN COLUMN 7.

exercises.prompt: Which column makes a line a comment, with a *?
exercises.explanation: Columns 1-6 are for the sequence number, so the * comes right after them.

exercises.prompt: Where do statements like DISPLAY start?
options: In Area B, column 12 or later
exercises.explanation: Area A (8-11) is for headers and names.

exercises.prompt: This job doesn't compile. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explanation: DISPLAY starts in column 8, Area A. Statements belong in Area B: column 12.

exercises.prompt: Why did programmers punch sequence numbers into columns 1-6?
options: To sort a dropped card deck back into order
The compiler needs them to run
To count the lines for the bill
exercises.explanation: A deck of 2,000 cards on the floor was a disaster, unless they were numbered.

exercises.prompt: What happens to text after column 72?
options: It continues on the next line
exercises.explanation: Columns 73-80 were used for the program's name on each card.

lessons.title: Periods and Sentences
intro: A period ends a sentence, like in English. After the last statement of a paragraph, a period is a must. COBOL programmers say a missing period is the most expensive dot in the world.
DISPLAY can show several things in a row: texts and numbers are put together without spaces. DISPLAY "TOTAL: " 42 shows TOTAL: 42.
The old compilers only knew capital letters, and that's how COBOL is still written in most companies.

exercises.explanation: The parts are put together exactly as they are: the space is inside the quotes.

exercises.prompt: This job doesn't compile. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explanation: The program ends without a period after STOP RUN.

exercises.prompt: What does a period do in the PROCEDURE DIVISION?

exercises.explanation: Two texts in one DISPLAY are joined without a space.

exercises.prompt: Put the statements in order so the job shows 1, 2, 3 and ends.
exercises.explanation: Statements run from top to bottom.
